en.title: Brazil's Soft Power: Two Centuries of Diplomacy, Culture and Influence (1822–2026)
en.deck: From imperial recognition and Rio Branco to the UN, Mercosur, BRICS, G20 and COP30: why Brazil's cultural visibility exceeds its uneven ability to shape international outcomes.
en.regime: Long-run rise in institutional and cultural visibility, with intermittent geopolitical and economic constraints on effective influence.
en.key_risk: Conflating cultural popularity, survey perceptions, multilateral access and achieved diplomatic outcomes.
watch: Independent diplomacy and climate perception indicators

producer_checks.information_cutoff: 2026-11-11 America/Sao_Paulo; current policy/legal facts reverified against sources last updated 2026-11-03 and Brand Finance June 2026.
producer_checks.source_check: 20 traceable sources, primarily official FUNAG, UN, government, UNESCO, ABC, G20, Siscomex and one explicit perception-index publisher; each instrument distinguished from inference.
producer_checks.historical_method: 205 individual years, 1822-2026; dated events separated from years described only by period context to avoid unsupported fabricated annual milestones. Soft power retrospective label, not nineteenth-century self-description.
producer_checks.argument_continuity: Stages: attraction versus outcomes → empire → territorial legalism → world order → autonomy and legitimacy → democratization → South–South coalitions → recent setbacks → 2023–2026 and constraints → mechanisms/comparators/falsifiers.
producer_checks.visual_evidence: Both locales: one 5-row comparison table, one bar chart of UN Security Council mandate starts 1940s–2020s, one four-chain causal flow and one six-region geographical exposure map. Chart data 1,2,2,0,1,2,1,1,1 identical.
producer_checks.bilingual_parity: English primary edition ~8,000 words and PT-BR ~8,600 words; 15 substantive numbered sections, 205 annual entries, 20 identical source URLs and equivalent visuals, arguments and conclusions.
producer_checks.editorial_status: Producer-staged only, no public report created; independent SHA-bound QA and publisher required.

contrary_evidence: Brand Finance survey measures perceptions and rankings, not causal policy effectiveness or a comparable historical soft-power time series.
Military interventions in the Empire and the peacekeeping mission in Haiti involved coercion, contested local legitimacy and human costs.
Brazil's 2019–2022 diplomatic disagreements did not prevent election to its eleventh Security Council term in 2022–2023.
The 2026 Mercosur–EU provisional trade application is not full definitive ratification of the partnership.
Event hosting at G20, BRICS and COP30 does not establish policy implementation or realized financing.
Brazil's culture can be globally recognizable while political influence remains bounded by veto powers, industrial dependence and domestic institutional credibility.
limitations: The chronology does not establish a unique diplomatic event for every single year; unmarked years explicitly retain period context.
Brand Finance index is a proprietary cross-sectional perception instrument; it should not be projected backwards to 1822.
The report does not estimate a synthetic index of historical soft power or an unobservable causal effect of music and sport on diplomatic votes.
Some nineteenth-century historical background relies on documentary historical syntheses rather than a separate primary archive for each year.
Impacts of COP30 decisions, the anti-hunger alliance and Mercosur–EU remain to be verified by future implementation metrics.
News after 11 November 2026 is outside the factual cutoff.
Independent QA, source-hash approval and public site deployment have not yet occurred at producer stage.
